title: Review: Alkenes: electrophilic addition; Sigma/pi, hybridisation and resonance; formal charge; Halogenoalkanes: nucleophilic substitution
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for Edexcel A-level Chemistry (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: OR09#t4 term and clue written for the game; BD07#t2 term and clue written for the game; OR09#t1 term and clue written for the game; BD07#t1 term and clue written for the game. Questions: BD07#N.5, OR09#N.3, OR12#N.16, BD07#N.13, OR09#N.12, OR12#N.6, OR09#N.14, OR12#N.11, OR09#N.9, OR12#N.14, OR09#N.6, OR12#N.2. Some questions repeat from the worlds it reviews.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Hydrolysis
items.clue: Another name for substitution of a halogenoalkane by OH⁻, giving an alcohol.

items.label: Pi bond
items.clue: Sideways overlap of two p orbitals, with electron density above and below the axis.

items.label: Nucleophile
items.clue: An electron-pair donor, attracted to a δ+ atom; OH⁻, CN⁻, NH₃ and H₂O are examples.

items.label: Sigma bond
items.clue: Direct, head-on overlap of orbitals, with electron density on the axis between the nuclei.

questions.stem: A student suggests that a π bond between two carbon atoms prevents rotation about the bond that joins them. Which observation does this hypothesis predict?

options.text: ClHC=CHCl exists as two separable compounds
ClH₂C–CH₂Cl exists as two separable compounds
H₂C=CHCl exists as two separable compounds
ClC≡CCl exists as two separable compounds

questions.explanation: With no rotation, the two Cl atoms are fixed on the same side or opposite sides of C=C: two isomers. ClH₂C–CH₂Cl has no π bond, so it rotates and is one compound.

questions.stem: Which set contains only species that can act as nucleophiles?

options.text: OH⁻, H⁺, Br⁻
NH₃, H₂O, CN⁻
Cl⁻, NO₂⁺, H₂O
OH⁻, CN⁻, CH₄

questions.explanation: Each has a lone pair to donate: on N in NH₃, on O in H₂O, on C in CN⁻. A nucleophile need not be charged.

questions.stem: In the dark, at room temperature, but-2-ene quickly decolourises a solution of iodine monochloride, ICl. Butane does not react with it. The product is CH₃CHICHClCH₃. Which statement explains why but-2-ene reacts without light?

options.text: The C=C bond is weaker than a C–C single bond, so it breaks easily without needing any light.
The electron-rich C=C donates a pair to Iδ+, and the I–Cl bond breaks heterolytically.
ICl splits into I• and Cl• radicals even in the dark, and these radicals attack only C=C bonds.
The carbon atoms of the C=C bond are electron-deficient, so they attract the Clδ− end of ICl.

questions.stem: Mean (average) bond enthalpies: C–C 347 kJ mol⁻¹ · C=C 612 kJ mol⁻¹ · C≡C 838 kJ mol⁻¹. A C≡C bond is only about 2.4 times as strong as a C–C bond, not 3 times. Which statement explains this?

options.text: Its three shared pairs repel one another, so C≡C is longer than C–C.
All three of its bonds are σ bonds, but they are weaker because they share space.
Two of its three bonds come from sideways overlap of p orbitals, which is less effective.
Its π electrons lie on the axis between the nuclei, where σ electrons repel them.

questions.explanation: C≡C is one σ and two π. Each π adds less than a σ: 612 − 347 = 265, then 838 − 612 = 226. So the total is well below 3 × 347 = 1041.

questions.stem: Bromoethane is heated with excess ammonia in ethanol: CH₃CH₂Br + 2NH₃ → CH₃CH₂NH₂ + NH₄Br. What does the second NH₃ molecule do?

options.text: It attacks the δ+ carbon again, so two NH₃ add to each carbon.
It supplies the two H atoms of the NH₂ group in the amine.
It reacts directly with Br⁻ to make NH₄Br.
It acts as a base, removing H⁺ from the CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺ ion.

questions.explanation: The first NH₃ is the nucleophile, giving CH₃CH₂NH₃⁺. The second uses its lone pair to take H⁺, giving the amine and NH₄⁺.

questions.stem: Ethene is bubbled through a solution of bromine in an organic solvent at room temperature, in the dark. Which statement is correct?

options.text: The bromine loses its colour as CH₂BrCH₂Br forms by addition.
The bromine loses its colour as CH₂=CHBr forms by substitution.
No reaction occurs, as Br₂ has no positive charge.
No reaction occurs, as UV light is needed to split Br₂.

questions.explanation: Br₂ adds across the C=C bond: CH₂=CH₂ + Br₂ → CH₂BrCH₂Br. The orange-brown colour of bromine disappears; this is the test for C=C.

questions.stem: Iodoethane, CH₃CH₂I, is warmed with aqueous sodium hydroxide, and ethanol forms. Which statement about the electron pairs is correct?

options.text: One electron from O and one from C form the C–O bond; I leaves as an atom, I•.
A lone pair on O forms the C–O bond; the C–I pair leaves with I, as I⁻.
The C–I pair moves across to O to become the C–O bond; I leaves as I⁺.
A lone pair on O attacks the δ− iodine atom, and the C–I pair moves onto carbon.

questions.explanation: OH⁻ is the nucleophile: its lone pair goes to the δ+ carbon. The C–I bond breaks heterolytically, and I⁻ leaves.

questions.stem: 2,3-dimethylbut-2-ene, (CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)₂, reacts with hydrogen bromide. What is the product?

options.text: (CH₃)₂CBr–CBr(CH₃)₂
(CH₃)₂C=C(CH₃)CH₂Br
(CH₃)₂CH–CH(CH₃)₂
(CH₃)₂CH–CBr(CH₃)₂

questions.explanation: HBr adds across C=C: H to one carbon, Br to the other. The double bond becomes single. Both carbons are alike, so there is one product, 2-bromo-2,3-dimethylbutane.

questions.stem: 1-chlorobutane, 1-bromobutane and 1-iodobutane are each added to aqueous silver nitrate in ethanol at 50 °C. Which tube shows a precipitate first, and what colour is it?

options.text: 1-iodobutane; yellow
1-chlorobutane; white
1-iodobutane; cream
All three at once, as water attacks each carbon equally

questions.explanation: C–I (228 kJ mol⁻¹) is the weakest C–X bond, so I⁻ is released fastest. AgI is yellow.

questions.stem: Ethene reacts with hydrogen bromide by electrophilic addition. Which describes the curly arrows in the first step of the mechanism?

options.text: From the H atom of HBr to the C=C bond, and from Br to the H–Br bond
From the C=C bond to the Br of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to the H
From the C=C bond to the H of HBr, and from the H–Br bond to Br
Fish-hook arrows split H–Br into H• and Br•, which add to C=C

questions.explanation: The electron-rich C=C bond donates a pair to the δ+ H atom, forming a C–H bond, while the H–Br bonding pair moves onto Br. This gives CH₃CH₂⁺ and Br⁻; Br⁻ then bonds to the carbocation.

questions.stem: Hydroxide ions react with 1-chloropropane: CH₃CH₂CH₂Cl + OH⁻ → CH₃CH₂CH₂OH + Cl⁻. Which describes the curly arrows correctly?

options.text: One arrow from a lone pair on the O of OH⁻ to the Cl atom; one from the C–Cl bond to the Cl atom.
One arrow from the C atom to the O of OH⁻; one from the Cl atom to the C–Cl bond.
One arrow from a lone pair on the O of OH⁻ to the C bonded to Cl; one from the C–Cl bond to Cl.
One arrow from a lone pair on the O of OH⁻ to the C atom; one from the C–Cl bond to the C atom.

questions.explanation: The O lone pair forms the new C–O bond, and the C–Cl bonding pair moves onto Cl, which leaves as Cl⁻.

questions.stem: Which set contains only species that can act as electrophiles?

options.text: H⁺, NO₂⁺, OH⁻
Br₂, HBr, NH₃
H⁺, NO₂⁺, Br₂
NO₂⁺, H⁺, Cl⁻

questions.explanation: Each can accept an electron pair. H⁺ has no electrons, NO₂⁺ is positive and electron-deficient, and Br₂ accepts a pair from a C=C bond.
